title: Canada's First Spacewalk in Seven Years Will Boost Station Power
summary:
Canada's Joshua Kutryk and NASA's Anil Menon are scheduled to step outside the International Space Station at 8 a.m. ET on Thursday, October 29. It will be the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in seven years, and Kutryk's first-ever spacewalk. Menon has done three spacewalks before. The spacewalk should last about 6 hours and 45 minutes.

Their job is to boost the station's power supply. This is the first of two spacewalks, with the second expected no sooner than November 5, to install the seventh and eighth International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, called iROSAs. The new arrays lie on top of the station's decades-old arrays, which are naturally degrading with age. The first iROSA rolled out in 2021. Once all eight are installed and running, the station's power supply will rise from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts, a boost of roughly 30 percent.

Canadian technology will help. Canadarm2, the station's robotic arm, will support the spacewalk. Ground controllers moved it to the storage area of a SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft, which brought the two arrays up earlier this month. Canadarm2 picked the arrays up, moved them to a transporter, and even loosened bolts ahead of time. During the walk, Kutryk and Menon will slide an array off its transport rail, and Menon will stand on a Canadarm2 platform holding it while NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, working from inside, move the arm to the installation site for the 2A electrical-power channel.

Each array is about 10 feet long when folded and weighs 750 pounds on Earth, so NASA planned new maneuvers that rotate around the array's center of mass rather than the crew member, to make the work less tiring. Kutryk will move hand-over-hand to the site, where the pair will bolt the array onto the older array and release it so it unfolds from about 10 feet to around 20 feet. Flight director Garrett Hehn compared the arrays to a snap bracelet: magnets along the side let each one roll out steadily, a process taking about 10 minutes. The capsule communicator for both spacewalks is Canadian astronaut Jenni Gibbons.
why_it_matters: A reliable power supply keeps the station's experiments, life-support systems, and communications running, so upgrading its solar arrays protects the research astronauts do in orbit.

background_read: The International Space Station is a large laboratory that orbits Earth, where astronauts live and work for months at a time.
Solar arrays are panels that collect sunlight and turn it into electricity to power the station's lights, machines, and experiments.
Like many machines, older solar arrays grow weaker with age, so new ones are laid on top of them to restore the power supply.
A spacewalk means an astronaut leaves the station in a protective suit to do a job outside, often with help from a robotic arm and teammates inside.
